title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into per‑device configuration is a core NetOps task and a natural target for generative LLMs. Prior work demonstrates promising intent→configuration synthesis in controlled settings but also documents failure modes—ordering mistakes, omissions, and unsafe commands—that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Architectural proposals therefore advocate hybrid patterns that combine probabilistic generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops to provide operational floor‑safety. Despite these proposals, rigorous preregistered measurements that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics are scarce. We address this gap with a narrowly scoped paired experiment that isolates the incremental effect of (1) a frozen deterministic validator and (2) a single automated repair attempt on a single LLM‑proposed plan per task. The core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design?
sections.related_work: Recent literature on LLMs for NetOps reports system demonstrations and surveys of intent translation and configuration generation; these works show feasibility in lab/testbed settings but emphasize vendor/topology sensitivity and safety concerns [10.1002/nem.2313, 10.36227/techrxiv.177004277.71795055/v1]. Work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) documents that verifier‑assisted pipelines and retrieval‑augmented generation reduce factual errors and produce more grounded outputs, motivating guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification methods (e.g., header‑space/specification checking) provide algorithmic primitives for static validators that can check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Standards and evaluation reviews highlight the need for auditability and explicit evaluation protocols when LLMs are used in operations [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands by preregistering a paired generate→validate→repair evaluation with archived artifacts and confirmatory inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered study cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 before observing final outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses were (H1) the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation and (H2) one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly recorded the planning assumption used in power calculations: planned baseline pass rate = 0.40; this assumption is central to interpreting confirmatory power and is reported here.

Design and pairing semantics: We used a paired within‑task design on a deterministically generated seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed the pipeline produced a single shared LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate) that served as the baseline response and as the starting point for the guarded arm (validator ± repair). This pairing was preregistered to emulate operational workflows in which a single proposed plan is reviewed and possibly repaired; it increases ecological validity but reduces expected discordant counts relative to independent draws and therefore constrains McNemar‑style power for a given N.

Model and generation settings: The declared generator was gpt-5-mini. Execution accounting (archived) records model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). Important model‑configuration evidence: the archived execution/model_configuration.json records the model configuration used in the run and shows "temperature": null (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). A null/unset temperature is not equivalent to a deterministic temperature=0 setting; it indicates that sampling determinism was unspecified in the recorded configuration. Sampling nondeterminism (if present) affects generator variance and therefore the marginal distribution of proposals; because temperature was not fixed to enforce determinism, generator variance is an unresolved design factor in this run and is reported explicitly in the Disclosure Statement and in Methods to support accurate inference and reproduction.

Validator, scoring, and repair: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized responses to a normalized configuration AST and applied static rule/dependency checks derived from each task's workflow constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). The scoring rule was full intent‑constraint validation: pass only if the validator's normalized_configuration satisfies the task's required_sequence and expected_final_state and no violations remain. The preregistered repair adapter was invoked only when violations were reported; it was restricted to a single automated repair attempt per episode aimed at minimal edits that remove violations while preserving the original plan when allowed. Post‑repair configurations were revalidated by the same deterministic validator.

Analysis plan and estimands: The primary estimand was the absolute paired difference in per‑task success probability (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test at α=0.05; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with preregistered seed = 1729. Secondary analyses included exact binomial CIs for repair success conditional on initial failure and sensitivity treatments for failed provider calls. All per‑task artifacts, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, and analysis code were archived and are the authoritative sources for the reported numeric counts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301. No provider/infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic contamination exclusions were triggered.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. These counts are reproduced in the archived paired_contingency_table.csv artifact.

Inferential results (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.00 on the observed contingency. Observed absolute paired difference = (n10 − n01)/N = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes: the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 = [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty due to the single observation.

Artifact‑grounded sensitivity: The total observed discordant pairs (n10 + n01) = 1 imposes a hard bound on resolvable absolute paired differences equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Therefore the preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction starting from the planned baseline = 0.40, corresponding to an absolute +0.30) was not testable under the observed near‑ceiling baseline; detecting such a target would have required ≈90 net discordant pairs in favor of guarded outputs for N=300. The archived contingency artifact and bootstrap outputs support these statements.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation linked to artifacts. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) directly constrains inferential outcomes: with only one discordant pair the McNemar statistic lacks informative mass to reject the null for large preregistered effects, which explains the exact p = 1.00 and the narrow absolute improvement bound. This is an empirical consequence of (a) the observed near‑ceiling baseline and (b) the shared_initial_candidate pairing semantics that reduce expected discordant counts.

Lessons for planning confirmatory NetOps experiments. Power planning must jointly consider plausible baseline prevalence and pairing semantics. Shared‑candidate pairing improves ecological validity for remediation claims but reduces informative discordance; independent‑draws designs increase discordance for the same marginals but answer a different operational question. When H2 (repair effectiveness) is a focal claim, designers should ensure a planned number of initial failures (via task‑difficulty calibration or adversarial augmentation) so that the conditional estimator P(repair succeeds | initial failure) has acceptable precision.

Construct and external validity. Our validator performs deterministic static checks and canonicalization rather than dynamic emulation, so the results are conditional on validator semantics and do not measure runtime control‑plane/dataplane consequences (e.g., convergence transients). External generality is limited by the synthetic task bank and constrained vendor templates enumerated in the task manifest.

Operational implication. The run shows that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded repair loop can correct at least some invalid candidates automatically (observed correction 1/1), but when baseline errors are rare such a pipeline functions primarily as a safety net for infrequent mistakes rather than as a mechanism that substantially increases throughput. Organizations should align evaluation goals (error reduction vs catastrophic risk mitigation) with task selection, pairing semantics, and whether emulation is required for runtime guarantees.

Reproducibility and diagnostic practice. Deterministic canonicalization and structured validator traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) are essential for reproducible failure analysis. Our archived execution manifest, per‑task traces, and analysis artifacts (listed in the Disclosure Statement) enable recomputation of reported counts and intervals and support post‑hoc diagnostics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline composed of a frozen deterministic validator and one automated repair iteration. Observed counts: baseline 299/300 valid, guarded 300/300 valid; the guarded pipeline corrected the single invalid baseline output. The preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing power to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps studies should (1) calibrate task difficulty or augment adversarially to produce a planned number of initial failures/discordant pairs, (2) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (3) include emulation when runtime semantics are material. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Model sampling determinism was unspecified in the archival model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json records "temperature": null); null does not imply deterministic sampling and generator variance was therefore unresolved.

Validation used deterministic static configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
